Name: crosslingual_shared_store
Title: One Memory, Many Tongues: Language-Agnostic Storage With Per-Language Access
Short Hypothesis: Factual associations are stored in a largely language-agnostic mid-layer representation, while language-specific input encoding and output decoding wrap this shared store; consequently, a fact learned in one language is decodable from another language's query at middle layers even when the model cannot produce it in that language. Retrieval failure across languages is an access/verbalization problem, not a storage gap.
Related Work: Cross-lingual factual consistency is studied behaviorally (Jiang et al., 2020; multilingual LAMA) and some work finds shared multilingual subspaces (Wendler et al., 2024, 'English as pivot'). We specifically test the storage-vs-access decomposition: that facts reside in a shared store decodable cross-lingually at mid layers, isolating where cross-lingual transfer breaks-input, store, or output.
Abstract: Multilingual models answer factual questions inconsistently across languages, but it is unclear whether this reflects language-specific storage or shared storage with fragile access. We hypothesize a shared, language-agnostic factual store in middle layers, wrapped by language-specific input and output processing. We test this by (i) training an attribute probe on English recall states and evaluating whether it decodes the correct object from residual states produced by same-fact queries in other languages at matched mid layers; (ii) checking that decodability persists even when the model's surface answer in that language is wrong, indicating a verbalization rather than storage failure; and (iii) causally patching mid-layer states from a language where recall succeeds into one where it fails, testing whether the answer is rescued. We evaluate across several languages and relations, quantifying a storage-sharing index and a verbalization-gap. If facts are decodable cross-lingually even when unsayable, cross-lingual inconsistency is an access problem, implying that multilingual factual reliability can be improved by strengthening decoding pathways rather than re-teaching facts per language. The framework localizes where cross-lingual transfer succeeds or fails along the input-store-output pipeline.
Experiments: 1. Build parallel factual queries across languages with shared triples. 2. Train an attribute probe on English mid-layer states; evaluate cross-lingual decoding on other-language queries. 3. Split other-language items into surface-correct vs surface-wrong; test decodability in the surface-wrong subset (verbalization gap). 4. Cross-lingual activation patching from success to failure; measure rescue. Metrics: cross-lingual probe accuracy, storage-sharing index, verbalization-gap size, patching rescue rate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Entity tokenization differs across languages, complicating position matching and probing. Probes trained in English may capture English-specific features. Some facts may genuinely be stored per-language for low-resource languages. Patching across languages may inject language identity, confounding rescue.
